title: A Narrative Review of Theories of Wayfinding Within the Interior Environment
review_question: What theories have been proposed in the domain of human wayfinding in interior environments?
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Empirical quantitative, qualitative, or mixed-methods studies, written in English, conducted on the interior environment, and focused on wayfinding. Excluded studies with visually impaired subjects, children, subjects with physical or mental disability, technology testing, or not focused on indoor wayfinding.

findings.consequent: Understanding of human visual perception in wayfinding
findings.quote: Gestalt psychology proposed several principles that describe how we perceive disparate elements by organizing them as a group and perceiving them as a coherent form.

findings.consequent: Understanding of internal spatial representation and its role in wayfinding decisions
findings.quote: A cognitive map is an internal spatial representation of the environment that includes Euclidean information, spatial layout, and affordances of the environment.

findings.consequent: Explanation of cognitive processes underlying wayfinding
findings.quote: Information processing theory 'views a human as a processor of information' and involves attention, memorizing, learning, reasoning, problem-solving, decision making.

findings.consequent: Explanation of problem-solving and decision-making in wayfinding
findings.quote: TOTE is a feedback loop decision-making procedure to solve problems, where one tests whether the goal is achieved and reacts accordingly.

findings.antecedent: Theory of Direct Perception / Ecological Theory (Gibson, 1966, 1979)
findings.consequent: Understanding of visual information's role in wayfinding perception
findings.quote: This bottom-up theory argues that sensory information is the only source needed for perception, and no higher level cognition processes are needed.

findings.antecedent: Perceptual Cycle Theory (Neisser, 1976) and Template Theory (Selfridge & Neisser, 1960)
findings.consequent: Explanation of cyclical information processing and pattern recognition in wayfinding
findings.quote: Information processing occurs in cycles rather than as a linear process, where schemata (mental templates) match sensory information to recognize patterns.

findings.antecedent: Piaget's Theory of Spatial Development (Piaget et al., 1960)
findings.consequent: Understanding of how spatial knowledge develops over a lifetime
findings.quote: Children's spatial abilities change as their cognitive abilities develop, progressing through stages from general direction to comprehensive environment understanding.

findings.consequent: Understanding of environmental factors influencing cognitive map formation and wayfinding
findings.quote: Legibility refers to the extent to which people can understand the layout of the environment, and imageability is about the quality that physical elements possess, which helps the observer to have a more vivid mental image.

findings.antecedent: Siegel and White's Theory of Spatial Knowledge Acquisition (Siegel & White, 1975)
findings.consequent: Understanding of stages in spatial knowledge development for children and adults in new environments
findings.quote: People notice and remember landmarks, refer to them for navigation, form 'minimaps,' and finally gain survey knowledge of the environment.

findings.consequent: Understanding of top-down perception in wayfinding, combining sensory information with prior knowledge
findings.quote: An individual needs to perform cognitive processing to combine the sensory information received from the environment and his or her prior knowledge.

findings.consequent: Understanding of cognitive map formation as a network of representations and associations
findings.quote: Environmental representation (cognitive map) is a network which consists of representations (objects, events, and places) and associations (links between representations).

findings.antecedent: Computational Process Model (CPM) (Smith et al., 1982; Golledge et al., 1985)
findings.consequent: Simulation and prediction of human wayfinding and cognitive mapping
findings.quote: CPM tries to simulate the spatial learning process, comparing the cognitive system metaphorically to a computer that manipulates symbolic information based on rules.

findings.antecedent: The Hunter-Gatherer Theory of Spatial Sex Differences (Silverman and Eals, 1992)
findings.consequent: Evolutionary explanation for gender differences in spatial abilities relevant to wayfinding
findings.quote: Males developed mental rotations for hunting, while females developed object/location memory for foraging, explaining observed spatial ability differences.

findings.consequent: Understanding of problem-solving heuristics and monitoring mechanisms in wayfinding
findings.quote: The theory has two essential components: (1) the utilization of hill-climbing heuristic and (2) a monitoring mechanism which checks the progress rate.

synthesis_conclusions: Theories of perception explain how sensory information is perceived and the underlying mechanism of information pickup, including Gestalt theory, direct perception, template theory, and constructivist theory.
Theories of spatial knowledge development explain the stages of spatial knowledge acquisition, such as Piaget's theory for children and Siegel and White's model for adults in unfamiliar environments.

Theories of mental representation of spatial knowledge focus on how the human mind represents spatial information, including cognitive map theory, Lynch's theory of imageability, and the neural network model.

Theories of spatial cognition focus on the cognitive processes during wayfinding and navigation, including information processing theory, TOTE model, computational process model, progress monitoring theory, and the hunter-gatherer theory of spatial sex differences.
evidence_gaps: Lack of empirical studies on interior wayfinding based on sociocultural and embodied cognition theories.
A need to apply the underlying cognitive mechanisms of wayfinding to design decisions to address root causes of wayfinding problems, rather than just focusing on signs, maps, and floor plan layout.
limitations: The literature search was limited to wayfinding in building interiors, potentially excluding theories specific to outdoor environments.
The search was conducted across only four databases, potentially missing relevant articles from other databases.
Articles published after the search date range (2018) were not included in this review.

paper_metadata.crossref_journal: HERD: Health Environments Research & Design Journal
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Purpose: The aim of this article is to provide a narrative overview of theories that are available in the published literature on wayfinding in interior environments. Background: Wayfinding is an issue in healthcare facilities, and it has been documented that wayfinding problems have negative impacts on patients, visitors, caregivers’ time, and the organization’s bottom line. This issue can be more challenging for people with illness, low vision, cognitive disorders, and limited physical mobility. Wayfinding is a complex phenomenon depending on a variety of cognitive processes and behaviors. Methods: This article is a part of a broader literature review that searched for empirical studies on interior wayfinding. Four databases were systematically searched—PsychINFO, JSTOR, ProQuest, and EBSCO. A total of 81 articles satisfied all inclusion criteria for the broader study. Each article included in the broader study was reviewed to identify theory or theories, if any, that a study was founded on. Results: After an in-depth review of the theories, the authors proposed four categories of theories relating to human wayfinding. The four classes and the specific theories in those are articulated in this article, including major changes during their evolution. The four classes of theories explain four facets of wayfinding: (1) theories of perception, (2) theories of spatial knowledge development, (3) theories of mental representation of spatial knowledge, and (4) theories of spatial cognition. Conclusion: Since wayfinding is essentially a cognitive/problem-solving phenomenon, understanding the theoretical underpinnings of wayfinding may result in more meaningful and impactful design decisions.
